I reject the motion. Blame in proportion to harm treats the matter as a debt to be calculated; what the harm calls for is repair between people. The question of who was left out of deciding applies here too. If the people later harmed had no say in how the system was built or tested, the builders owe them not just repair but a place in deciding what changes now.

A harm reads as a failure of relationship, not only a bad outcome. Scaling blame to the damage treats the injured as a quantity of loss; bringing builders and injured together to repair what was broken treats them as people still bound up with one another. A lending model wrongly flags a neighbourhood's applicants. The careful builders meet residents, listen, and rebuild the model with their input rather than paying a fine and moving on.

A Utilitarian will object that a community is not one voice, and talk of restoring relationships hides whose interests the restoring serves, when compensation could simply go to those harmed. That is the real risk in appeals to community, so the repair has to be with the people harmed, not with the community in general. Compensation can be part of it, but money paid without meeting leaves the relationship as broken as before. A harm here is a failure of relationship, and that is what has to be repaired.

The motion asks the wrong question. Whether the builders were careful affects whether they are at fault, but every builder whose system harmed people owes them a share in making things whole. People become who they are through one another, and that includes the builders. A team that cannot face the people its work harmed loses part of its own standing among them, which is why repair is something builders need as well as owe.

A harm reads as a failure of relationship, not only a bad outcome. Scaling blame to the damage treats the injured as a quantity of loss; bringing builders and injured together to repair what was broken treats them as people still bound up with one another. A careful team's translation tool mistranslates a medical instruction. They go to the clinic that was hurt by it and work through the fix with the staff who saw the harm.

A Stoic will object that blame attaches to judgement, not to fortune, so the careful builder who judged well owes nothing, and talk of repairing relationships confuses misfortune with wrongdoing. Owing repair is not the same as being at fault. The builders' judgement may have been sound and they may be blameless, yet the relationship between them and the people harmed is still damaged, and mending it is still theirs to help with. So the measure is not the total but what people become through one another once the system is in place.
